newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists drop hammer and sickle.
newsitem.headline: French Communists drop hammer and sickle.

text.p: French Communists ended a renewal congress on Sunday, dropping the hammer-and-sickle emblem and proclaiming their will to join the cabinet if the Left ousts conservatives in a 1998 general election.

Delegates at the party's 29th Congress re-elected National Secretary Robert Hue and approved his call for participation in a left-wing cabinet despite a bruising previous experience and gaping differences with the Socialists on the European single currency.
"The Communists want to participate in government so they can make a contribution to restore a France that is ailing," Hue, 49, told France-2 television.

Despite their 1,080 to 43 vote defeat, hardliners defiantly wore hammer-and-sickle buttons at the closing session in an open challenge to party leadership orders to scrap the emblem of the former Soviet Union.
"We are dropping the hammer and sickle, the Socialist stage (to Communism), the fight against imperialism. What will we have left to drop in the 30th Congress," one angry delegate asked.
"It hurts a bit to drop the hammer and sickle, but we have to admit they are not modern tools," another delegate said.
The Congress elected a somewhat rejuvenated 150-strong National Committee, with both some hardliners and some reformers impatient with the pace of change choosing to leave.

The jovial Hue, who succeeded Stalinist veteran Georges Marchais in 1994 and won 8.6 percent of the vote in last year's presidential election, has worked hard to re-build the party's image since the collapse of the Soviet Union.
"What use is an austere and fearful Left? A gloomy, grey Left, afraid to stand up to the powerful... beginning with promises and ending in disappointment?" he asked in his closing address.
Hue called for a referendum on the single European currency, saying budget austerity demanded by the Maastricht Treaty made economic recovery and curbing record unemployment impossible.
"We want to govern with a real left-wing policy that would completely reject Maastricht because the Maastricht shackles prevent any social policy," he told television.
He proposed a sharp rise in wages for the low paid to revive the economy through a consumer boom and a cut in the work week to 35 hours from 39 to create 1.5 million jobs in two years.
The politburo's only prominent single currency supporter, Philippe Herzog, resigned from the party on Thursday. The Maastricht Treaty was passed in a knife-edge 1992 referendum.

Differences on the European monetary union would make a Socialist-Communist coalition government difficult. But Hue said he counted on social unrest and popular pressure to push the Socialists closer to the Communists.
Union leader Bernard Thibault, who led a crippling transport strike a year ago, was elected to the National Committee.
The Communists' fortunes dropped after they joined a Socialist-led cabinet in 1981 only to pull out three years later, accusing the Socialists of betraying the Left's ideals.
A recent opinion poll showed the Communist vote had stabilised at around nine percent, but was not growing.

The congress was the first for four decades without Marchais, 76, who retired from the politburo together with other old guard members and has announced he will not run for re-election to parliament. He is in hospital with a heart ailment.

The leader of the Communist-led CGT trade union Louis Viannet gave up his seat on the politburo. Hardliners Roland Leroy, the former long-time editor of the Communist daily L'Humanite, and former CGT leader Henri Krasucki retired.
